Maladaptive Strategies.value: I think about why the event has happened to me
I try hard to control my emotions

Memory.value: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

Negative Appraisals.value: The people responsible have faced no consequences
I have to be on guard all the time

vignette: Meera was twelve when the pattern cemented itself. She remembered kitchen tiles cold against her knees, the heavy thud of a cane striking linoleum, and the metallic tang of fear that coated her tongue. Her caregiver never explained the violence, and over time, Meera came to believe that his absence from any reckoning meant the abuse was simply accepted. That early lack of consequence, paired with her parents' bitter divorce, taught her she could not trust any place to hold her safely. She drifted through marriages and cities until she settled alone in a Houston studio, surrounded by cameras and the sharp scent of fixer. Over decades, she learned to stand on guard everywhere she went, shoulders perpetually braced for a strike. Her conviction that accountability was absent and that she belonged nowhere directly shaped how the trauma memories surfaced. Rather than allowing them to integrate, these appraisals kept the past fragmented; when she tried to deliberately recall what happened, she found she could not access the memory at all. This unresolved belief system fed directly into her need to question why the violence targeted her, driving her to search for a logic that never emerged. In response, she learned to cover her face with her hands and rigidly control her emotional display. These very strategies, in turn, dictated her recollection. By actively suppressing her reactions, she made deliberate access impossible, yet when her guard finally slipped, the memories that broke through carried the exact terror she felt as a child, immediately followed by crushing shame. Now in her seventies, Meera's life revolves around a gallery space she rents above a South Asian grocery. Her work once felt like a refuge, but lately, the studio became a trigger. Last month, a delivery driver dropped a heavy lens case against the concrete floor. The thud matched the cane striking tiles so closely that she immediately dropped her tongs, pressing her palms flat over her mouth and holding her breath until the driver asked if she was alright. Controlling her body then-still, silent, face hidden-mirrored how she survived then. But silence did not stop the past from intruding. Because she had long accepted she belonged nowhere, the sudden intimacy with a stranger felt unbearable. She excused herself to the restroom, sat on the cold tile, and tried to steady her chest while shame threatened to pull her under. What finally pushed Meera to seek help was the slow erosion of her work. She could no longer attend gallery viewings without scanning exits and monitoring conversation volume. The exhaustion of maintaining that perimeter outweighed her pride. She now hoped someone might finally help her understand why the past refused to stay buried. She feared the terror would continue hijacking her days, but she also hoped that in a safe space, she might finally remember without shame.
